text: Richard Stallman is a computer scientist and software freedom advocate born in 1953 in New York City. He earned a bachelor's degree in physics from Harvard University and worked at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, where he developed software like Emacs and contributed to the development of the GNU project. In 1983, he announced the GNU project, aiming to create a free and open-source operating system compatible with Unix. He founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) to promote free software and introduced the concept of copyleft, notably through the GNU General Public License (GPL), which ensures software can be freely used, modified, and distributed. Stallman contributed key tools to the GNU system, including the GNU Emacs text editor, GCC compiler, and GNU Debugger. He is a strong critic of proprietary software, arguing that users should have the freedom to study, modify, and share software. His activism includes opposing software patents, digital rights management (DRM), and restrictive licensing. He also advocates for reduced copyright and supports free software in education and public institutions. Stallman has been a vocal critic of surveillance and has promoted user privacy. He is known for his principled stance on software freedom, including refusing to autograph items with a copyright symbol. In 2019, he faced controversy over comments related to the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, leading to his resignation from MIT and the FSF, though he later returned to the FSF board. He lives in Boston and is an atheist of Jewish ancestry, speaking English, French, Spanish, and Indonesian. Stallman has received numerous honors, including the MacArthur Fellowship and the ACM Software System Award. He is also known for his work on free software and his advocacy for user freedom, including his diagnosis with follicular lymphoma in 2023, which he later stated he was in remission from.
